prompt: What is the most direct fix for the outage?
scenario: An API service has one shared pool of 250 worker threads. It handles 500 requests a second; 20% of them call a fraud-scoring service. Fraud scoring starts hanging until a 4-second timeout, and within seconds every endpoint, including health checks, times out.

options.text: Raise the shared pool to 1,000 threads so there is room for the hung fraud calls
Give fraud scoring its own bounded pool and fail fast or fall back when it is full
Add a per-client rate limit at the gateway so no caller can send over 100 requests/s
Autoscale the API fleet on CPU so new instances absorb the extra hung requests

explanation: Fraud calls need 100/s × 4 s = 400 threads, more than the pool, so they drain it and starve every other endpoint. A bulkhead caps how many threads fraud can hold, so the rest keep working. 1,000 threads only delays exhaustion (still 400 hung plus a memory cost) and leaves the coupling in place. A per-client rate limit does not reduce calls to fraud scoring; total traffic is unchanged. Hung threads use almost no CPU, so CPU-based autoscaling may never trigger, and new instances fill the same way.

prompt: A dependency receives 150 calls a second with a p99 latency of 200 ms. Using Little's law with 2× headroom, what bulkhead limit fits?

options.text: About 15 concurrent calls
About 30 concurrent calls
About 60 concurrent calls
About 300 concurrent calls

explanation: Normal in-flight = 150 × 0.2 = 30; with 2× headroom that is 60. 30 is the steady-state figure with no headroom, so ordinary bursts would be rejected. 15 halves the steady state and would reject healthy traffic constantly. 300 is the call rate times 2 with the latency ignored; it would let a hang tie up far more threads than needed.

prompt: Why can a semaphore bulkhead still leave the caller stuck when a dependency hangs, while a thread-pool bulkhead need not?

options.text: A semaphore only counts calls; the caller's own thread makes the call and waits unless it has a timeout
Semaphores are released only when the process restarts, so hung permits accumulate until a deploy
A semaphore bulkhead has no maximum, so it admits every call and the dependency's queue grows
Semaphores need a lock per call, and that lock blocks every other thread until the call returns

explanation: A semaphore bulkhead limits how many calls run, but each admitted call still runs on the caller's thread, so a hang holds that thread until a timeout fires. A thread-pool bulkhead runs the call on a separate thread, so the caller can stop waiting. Permits are released when the call finishes or times out, not only on restart. A semaphore bulkhead has a configured maximum; that is its whole purpose. Acquiring a permit is a cheap counter operation that does not block other threads for the call's duration.

prompt: A service has per-dependency bulkheads for all four of its downstreams. Which situations can still take it down? Select all that apply.

options.text: Incoming traffic triples and every pool is legitimately busy
The essential inventory dependency fails and has no fallback
All four pools share one database whose connections run out
An optional, fallback-equipped dependency starts hanging

explanation: Bulkheads contain one slow or failing dependency. Overall overload fills every pool at once and needs load shedding. An essential dependency without a fallback fails requests whether or not it is isolated. A resource shared outside the pools, such as one database, is not partitioned at all. A hanging optional dependency with a fallback is exactly the case a bulkhead handles: its pool fills, calls fail fast and the fallback runs.

prompt: What is happening, and what should change?
scenario: During a spike, a service's CPU is at 100% and it completes about 1,000 requests a second, its normal maximum. Yet clients report that almost every request fails. Clients use a 1-second timeout, and the server's request queue holds around 20,000 entries.

options.text: The CPU is too slow; move to larger instances so each request completes faster
Goodput collapse; cap the queue, drop expired requests and shed the excess early
The client timeout is too short; raise it to 30 s so that the queued work completes
A memory leak; restart instances on a schedule so that the queue is cleared often

explanation: 20,000 queued at 1,000/s is a 20-second wait, so every completion arrives after its client gave up: throughput is high, goodput is near zero. Bounding the queue, dropping requests past their deadline and rejecting the excess cheaply restores useful work. Larger instances help eventually but do nothing about a queue that already guarantees timeouts. A 30-second timeout makes users wait 20 seconds and holds more resources per request. Nothing points to a leak; the queue is explained by arrival rate exceeding capacity, and restarts would drop the work anyway, uncontrolled.

prompt: With priority-based shedding, roughly what share of cart requests succeed?
scenario: A service's capacity is 1,200 requests a second. During a spike it receives 400/s CRITICAL_PLUS payment requests, 1,000/s CRITICAL cart requests and 800/s SHEDDABLE analytics beacons. It sheds strictly from the lowest criticality up.

options.text: About 55%, the same share as every other class
About 80%, since payments take 400 of the 1,200
100%, since only analytics beacons are shed here
About 40%, since cart is shed before payments are

explanation: All 800 beacons are shed first. Payments take 400 of the 1,200, leaving 800 for 1,000 cart requests: 80% succeed. 55% is what uniform shedding would give (1,200 ÷ 2,200), which is exactly what priority avoids. Shedding only beacons leaves 1,400 requests for 1,200 capacity, so some cart requests must also go. 40% would require shedding cart down to 400, which wastes 400 units of capacity.

prompt: A service sheds 30% of requests during a spike, yet its offered load keeps rising. What is the most likely reason?

options.text: Clients retry shed requests immediately, so each rejection comes back as more load
Shedding raises latency for admitted requests, and so more clients join the queue
The 503 responses are cached by the CDN, which then forwards copies to the origin
The load balancer counts rejected requests twice when it weighs the instances

explanation: A rejection only removes load if the client waits before trying again; instant retries multiply offered load, which is why shedding must be paired with backoff, Retry-After and retry budgets. Shedding lowers latency for admitted requests, it does not raise it. A cached 503 would reduce origin traffic, not forward copies. Load balancer accounting does not create new requests at the service.

prompt: Why does a queue switch to LIFO under overload in Facebook's adaptive LIFO approach?

options.text: LIFO is cheaper to implement than FIFO, which matters when CPU is at its limit
The newest requests' clients are still waiting, unlike the oldest ones' clients
LIFO guarantees fairness, giving each client an equal share of the capacity
LIFO lets the server batch requests from the same client and save round trips

explanation: In a standing queue the oldest requests have probably passed their clients' timeouts, so serving the newest first keeps goodput up. Push and pop costs are the same for LIFO and FIFO. LIFO is deliberately unfair: old requests may never be served. It has nothing to do with batching by client.

prompt: Which control fits this problem best?
scenario: Every tenant of a multi-tenant API stays within its 200 requests-a-second quota. Even so, when 40 large tenants peak together the service's latency triples and timeouts begin. Capacity changes week to week as the team ships optimisations.

options.text: Lower every tenant's quota to 100 requests/s so the total sum fits the capacity
Raise every tenant's quota, since their requests are within the agreed limits
An adaptive concurrency limit that cuts admissions when latency starts to rise
A per-tenant token bucket so that each tenant's bursts are smoothed over time

explanation: This is server overload with every client inside its quota: admission control based on the server's own state is the fit, and an adaptive limit keeps up as capacity changes. Halving quotas punishes tenants all the time to handle a rare peak, and still needs re-tuning as capacity changes. Raising quotas makes overload worse. Per-tenant token buckets are rate limiting; each tenant already conforms, so they would admit the same total load.

prompt: With client-side adaptive throttling (K = 2), a client sent 1,000 requests in the window and the backend accepted 400. What rejection probability does the client apply locally?

options.text: About 0.6, the share the backend did not accept
Zero, since the backend is still accepting some
About 0.4, matching the backend's accept ratio

explanation: The formula is max(0, (requests − K × accepts) / (requests + 1)) = (1,000 − 800) / 1,001 ≈ 0.2. 0.6 is the backend's rejection rate, not the formula's output; K lets some excess through so the backend can signal recovery. The probability is zero only when requests are at most K × accepts. 0.4 is the accept ratio, which the formula does not use directly.

prompt: To keep rejection cheap, which checks belong before any database call? Select all that apply.

options.text: Has the request's propagated deadline already passed?
Is the client over its rate-limit quota right now?
Is in-flight work at the concurrency limit for this band?
Does the requested record exist in the primary table?

explanation: Deadline, quota and concurrency checks need only in-memory state, so they can reject work for microseconds of CPU before anything expensive runs. Checking whether a record exists is itself a database query, which is exactly the work admission control is meant to avoid spending on requests it will reject.
